title: The Imagined School
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart builds on Matthew Evans's idea of the "imagined school" and Russell Hobby's point that truth does not rise to the top to argue that school leaders routinely act on a mental model of their school that diverges from reality. He catalogues seven traps: assuming messages were understood, requested actions were done, planned curriculum was taught and learned, data is accurate, staff are behind initiatives, advocated teaching strategies are embedded, and stated values are shared. The danger, following Evans, is that decisions made for the imagined school pick the wrong problem and the wrong solution, provoking eye rolls at best and driving staff away at worst. Hart's remedies go beyond simply being visible: check colleagues' understanding explicitly (for example after lesson feedback), map the intended, taught and learned curriculum, assume data is inaccurate, sharpen purpose into a strategy hierarchy, actively invite and act on challenge, and do fewer things better. The piece treats leadership humility about what one cannot see as a practical discipline rather than a disposition.
points: The expert knowledge gap means leaders who have thought a message through assume others share their understanding, so Hart recommends asking recipients to explain back what they heard instead of asking "Does that make sense?"

Hart argues that dropped actions are information: if requests fall away it may be because they do not affect outcomes, add workload or clash with colleagues' values, all of which leaders should take seriously.
Leaders should run proposed actions through the filter "What if the data is incorrect?", since borderline scores grouped into cohort figures create a rose-tinted view of attainment.

Surface agreement may be people telling leaders what they want to hear, so challenge must be explicitly sought (for example via stop/start/continue), structured into the calendar, and visibly acted upon.
Initiative overload widens the gap between imagined and real school; if everything is a priority nothing is, so leaders should do less, better, and match priorities to the rhythm of the year.
quotes: Matthew Evans wrote a blog post a while back about the way we construct our own imagined school in our mind, warning us that the gap between how the school is and how we imagine it to be is where poor leadership thrives. I’ve been thinking about this a lot recently, combining this idea with Russell Hobby’s assertion that truth doesn’t always rise to the top; the idea that it is incredibly difficult for leaders to know the full reality of school life.

We have spent time thinking about it and give the message in a way that makes sense to us but for others receiving the message, who have not done all that thinking and discussion, the message might not be clear at all. Worse, if we give the message by email or in person without giving the opportunity for those receiving to ask questions, to challenge or to respond, we can easily make the assumption that others hold a similar understanding to us.

We’d be fools to think that all the actions we ask of our team are complete, let alone complete to a standard that we might want. If the things that we have asked our team to do fall away, there is probably a good reason for that.

We might inquire into buy in, even having conversations about the merits of the initiative where colleagues speak positively about it. But what if they are saying what they want us to hear? This would of course indicate a possible cultural problem where a colleague might not want to speak their mind but again we would be foolish to think that everyone is behind everything that we do.

As Evans indicates, if we make decisions based on this school instead of the real school, we could get it spectacularly wrong, choosing the wrong problem to tackle and choosing the wrong solution too. At best we might get a sigh and an eye roll about how leaders don’t get it and at worst we could actively drive our team away.

Leaders can easily find themselves interacting with a small sample of the workforce and this can give a skewed perception of what our colleagues as a whole think and how they behave. But this must all come with an acknowledgement that we are unlikely to see for ourselves the full reality of our school.

When we’re analysing a set of data, we cannot accept it as absolute truth; we are all at risk of falling for the illusion of certainty from data that oversimplifies complex reality and averages out nuance and context into a more digestible format. So let’s assume our data is inaccurate when we’re making plans to act on the data that we have.
